title: Printing Variables and Formatting Numbers
summary: Mix text and variables in one line of output and control decimals and column widths with iomanip.
intro: Real output mixes words with values and needs tidy numbers: a fixed count of decimals, columns that line up, IDs padded with zeros. This lesson covers chaining variables into `std::cout` and the `<iomanip>` tools that format them.

steps.title: Mixing text and variables

example.title: Introducing Ada
example.prompt: Print a sentence about a person from three variables in one statement.
example.output: Ada is 36 years old and 1.68 m tall.
example.explanation: The statement alternates variables and string pieces. Every space between words lives inside a string piece such as `" is "`, and the final piece ends with the period and `\n`. The three variables print as text, a whole number, and a decimal without any conversion on your part.

practice.title: Order line
practice.prompt:
Print one order line built from four variables in a single statement.

1. Use the variables `product`, `quantity`, `price`, and `currency` that the starter declares.
2. Print the quantity, then ` x `, then the product name, then ` at `.
3. Print the currency character directly before the price with no space, then ` each` and a newline.

Expected output:

```text
3 x Notebook at $4.75 each
```
hints: Chain all four variables with `<<` and put the spaces inside the string pieces.
Write `<< currency << price` with nothing between them so the `$` touches the number.

steps.title: Fixed decimals with setprecision
steps.body:
By default `std::cout` prints a `double` with 6 *significant digits*, not 6 decimals, and drops trailing zeros. So `2.50` prints as `2.5` and `123456.7` rounds to `123457`. From about a million up, values switch to scientific notation: `1234567.891` prints as `1.23457e+06`, which means 1.23457 times 10 to the 6th. Very tiny values do the same.

To control decimals, include `<iomanip>` and send two manipulators to the stream:

```cpp
std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(2);
std::cout << 1234567.891 << '\n';  // 1234567.89
std::cout << 0.5 << '\n';          // 0.50
```

`std::fixed` means always use plain decimal notation, and `std::setprecision(n)` then means exactly `n` digits after the point, rounding the last one and padding with zeros. Without `std::fixed`, `setprecision` counts significant digits instead. Neither one changes how an `int` prints.

Both settings are *sticky*: they stay in effect for every later number on `std::cout` until you change them. That is why you usually set them once near the top of `main`. It also means you should print any default-formatted value first, before switching to fixed. Changing just the precision later, such as `std::setprecision(4)`, keeps fixed mode on.

> Rounding uses the stored binary value, so a value like 2.675 can print as 2.67. Pick values that are not exact halfway points.

example.title: Big totals and pi
example.prompt: Print a large total with default formatting and with 2 decimals, then print pi with 4 decimals.
example.explanation: The first line uses the default 6 significant digits, so the seven-digit whole part forces scientific notation. The second line turns on fixed mode with 2 decimals and the `.891` rounds to `.89`. Fixed mode is still on for the third line, so only the precision changes, and `3.14159265` rounds up to `3.1416`.

practice.title: Distances
practice.prompt:
Print a long distance twice and a marathon length once, with different formatting.

1. Print `distance` with default formatting.
2. Turn on `std::fixed` with 2 decimals and print `distance` again.
3. Change the precision to 1 and print `marathon`.

Expected output:

```text
9.87654e+06
9876543.21
42.2
```
hints: Print the default line first, because `std::fixed` stays on once you send it.
Fixed mode is still active for the last line, so `std::setprecision(1)` alone is enough.

steps.title: Aligned columns with setw
steps.body:
`std::setw(n)` from `<iomanip>` makes the *next* item take at least `n` characters, padding with spaces. It applies to that one item only, so repeat it before each value you want padded. A value longer than `n` is never cut. It just prints in full.

```cpp
std::cout << std::setw(6) << 42 << '|' << 7 << '\n';  // "    42|7"
```

By default the padding goes before the value, so text and numbers alike line up on the right. `std::left` puts the padding after the value, which suits text columns, and `std::right` puts it before, which lines up numbers by their last digit. Unlike `setw`, both are sticky.

`std::setfill(c)` changes the padding character, and it is sticky too. The common use is zero-padding:

```cpp
std::cout << std::right << std::setfill('0') << std::setw(3) << 7 << '\n';  // 007
```

Two gotchas follow from stickiness. If `std::left` is still on, `std::setfill('0') << std::setw(5) << 42` prints `42000`, so switch back to `std::right` first. And once you zero-pad, later `setw` calls also pad with zeros until you send `std::setfill(' ')`. Keep zero-padded values non-negative, since `-42` would print as `00-42`.

example.title: Price table and order number
example.prompt: Print a three row price table with aligned columns, then an order number padded to 5 digits.
example.explanation: Each row sets `std::left` for the name and `std::right` for the price, and repeats `std::setw` because it only covers the next item. The name fills 10 characters and the price fills 8, so the decimal points line up. On the last line `std::setfill('0')` pads `42` with zeros to 5 digits, while `"Order #"` prints plainly because no `setw` comes before it. `orderNumber` is an `int`, so the earlier `std::fixed` and `std::setprecision(2)` do not change it.

practice.title: Scoreboard and clock
practice.prompt:
Print a three row scoreboard with aligned columns, then a clock time with two-digit parts.

1. Print each player name left-aligned in width 8, followed by the score right-aligned in width 5: `Mia` 120, `Leo` 95, `Zoe` 7.
2. Print the time from `hours` and `minutes` as `07:05`, using `std::right`, `std::setfill('0')`, and `std::setw(2)` before each number.

Expected output:

```text
Mia       120
Leo        95
Zoe         7
07:05
```
hints: Follow the price table pattern with widths 8 and 5. The scores are whole numbers, so you need no `std::fixed` here.
`std::setw` covers only the next item, so write `std::setw(2)` again before `minutes`. The `':'` is not padded.

recap:
- Chain text and variables with `<<` and put every space inside a string piece.
- A `char` prints as its character, handy for symbols like `'$'`.
- Doubles print with 6 significant digits by default, so big values show as `1.23457e+06`.
- `std::fixed << std::setprecision(n)` from `<iomanip>` prints exactly `n` decimals, and both stay in effect.
- `std::setw(n)` pads only the next item. `std::left`, `std::right`, and `std::setfill(c)` stay in effect.
- Zero-pad with `std::right << std::setfill('0') << std::setw(n)`, and reset with `std::setfill(' ')` when you are done.
